```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 1) format(round(x, d), nsmall = d)
```

This vignette shows how to describe your own table to DietView. DietView needs
one thing from your data: one row per prey record, that is, one prey taxon
found in one stomach. Taxonomy, tables, figures and dashboards are all built
from that table and from a specification that says which column is which.

The example is the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the
package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed
with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`).

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
```

## One row per prey record

Column names are free. You do not rename your data; you declare once which
column plays which role. `ices_diet` is already in the long format DietView
expects:

```{r data}
dim(ices_diet)
names(ices_diet)
```

Prey columns come first (`prey_aphia_id` to `prey_length_cm`), then the haul
and the predator, repeated on every record of the same stomach. The table has
no `kingdom` to `species` columns. DietView adds them when you attach a
taxonomy, here the frozen lineage `ices_lineage` (see the vignette on WoRMS).

## Declaring roles with `dv_spec()`

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",   # WoRMS AphiaID, used first when present
  prey_name      = "prey_name",       # scientific name, used when there is no ID
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
```

The roles, what they do, and the ICES column that fills each one:

| Role | Required | Purpose | ICES column |
|---|---|---|---|
| `predator` | yes | the predator of each record; a grouping and display label | `predator_common` |
| `stomach` | yes | the stomach each record came from; must be unique across the whole table, because stomach counts count distinct identifiers | `stomach_id` |
| `prey_id` / `prey_name` | at least one | prey keys used to attach the taxonomy | `prey_aphia_id`, `prey_name` |
| `weight` | no | the weight share (%W) | `prey_weight_g` |
| `count` | no | number of individuals per record, for the numerical share (%N). Records without a count contribute nothing to %N, so unidentified material usually disappears from that view | `prey_count` |
| `digestion` | no | enables the digestion diagnostic | `digestion_label` |
| `covariates` | no | columns you want to compare diets across | `region`, `year`, `quarter` |
| `predator_latin` | no | used to look up identification photos | `predator_latin` |

Columns you do not declare are kept and travel with the data: `length_cm`,
`country` or `ices_rectangle` can be added as covariates later, or used to
build new ones, such as length classes (see the dashboard vignette). For the
digestion role we use the readable `digestion_label` rather than the code
`digestion_stage`, because it also says where the stage was not recorded. Its
labels are inferred from the older ICES format; check them against the ICES
vocabulary before you rely on them.

## What counts as a prey record

```{r item-type}
table(ices_diet$item_type)
```

`item_type` sorts the records into three kinds. `prey` records carry a WoRMS
AphiaID. `unidentified` records are food that could not be named; they have no
AphiaID, and DietView keeps them as unidentified at every rank, which is the
point of the package. `non_food` records are sand, stones, plastic and wood:
real observations, but not diet, so they are dropped before the analysis.

Nematodes are a different case. They do have an AphiaID, but in fish stomachs
they are mostly parasites of the fish rather than food. The lineage tells you
which records they are:

```{r filter}
# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]
c(nematoda = sum(phylum %in% "Nematoda"), kept = nrow(dat))
```

```{r lost, include = FALSE}
lost <- length(setdiff(unique(ices_diet$stomach_id), unique(dat$stomach_id)))
```

Both choices belong to the analyst, which is why the data keep these records
and the filter is written out in the code. Dropping them also removes
`r lost` stomachs whose only records were nematodes or non-food items.

## Empty stomachs live in `ices_stomachs`

A stomach with no prey has no prey record, so it has no row in `ices_diet`.
The companion table `ices_stomachs` has one row per sampled stomach, empty or
not:

```{r stomachs}
st <- ices_stomachs
st$status <- ifelse(st$stomach_id %in% ices_diet$stomach_id, "with prey records",
             ifelse(st$stomach_empty %in% 1, "flagged empty", "no record, no flag"))
table(st$status)
table(st$country, st$status)
```

```{r st-values, include = FALSE}
tb <- table(st$status)
se_noflag <- sum(st$country == "SE" & st$status == "no record, no flag")
cod_all <- sum(st$predator_common == "Atlantic cod")
```

Of the `r big(nrow(st))` stomachs, `r big(tb[["with prey records"]])` have at
least one record and `r big(tb[["flagged empty"]])` are flagged empty. The other
`r big(tb[["no record, no flag"]])` have no record and no flag: almost all
(`r big(se_noflag)`) are Swedish, and the Swedish data do not report the empty
flag, so these stomachs are most likely empty, but the data do not say so.

This matters for every per-stomach measure. DietView counts the stomachs it
sees, so the denominator of `dv_fo_table()` is the number of stomachs with at
least one record: frequency of occurrence among feeding fish, not among all
fish sampled. For cod, `ices_stomachs` holds `r big(cod_all)` stomachs, while
the prepared data below hold `r big(length(unique(dat$stomach_id[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod"])))`.
Use `ices_stomachs` for the proportion of empty stomachs or the number of fish
sampled per stratum.

## Records and counts

A record is not an individual. `prey_count` gives the number of prey
individuals behind each record, when it was reported:

```{r counts}
c(records = nrow(dat), individuals = sum(dat$prey_count, na.rm = TRUE),
  no_count = sum(is.na(dat$prey_count)))
tapply(is.na(dat$prey_count), dat$item_type, sum)
```

Declaring `count` lets you switch from shares of records to shares of
individuals (%N). For cod, the two currencies at class rank:

```{r currency}
cod  <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
t_rec <- dv_tree(prep_cod)
t_num <- suppressWarnings(dv_tree(prep_cod, currency = "numbers"))
by_rec <- t_rec[t_rec$rank == "Class", ]
by_num <- t_num[match(by_rec$id, t_num$id), ]
cmp <- data.frame(class = by_rec$label, parent = by_rec$parent,
                  records = round(by_rec$pct_occ, 1),
                  numbers = round(by_num$pct_occ, 1))
head(cmp[order(-cmp$records), ], 5)
```

```{r cur-values, include = FALSE}
num <- by_num$pct_occ[by_num$label == "Malacostraca"]
rec <- by_rec$pct_occ[by_rec$label == "Malacostraca"]
mal <- prep_cod$data$class %in% "Malacostraca"
mal_multi <- mean(prep_cod$data$prey_count[mal] > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Malacostraca rise from `r pct(rec)`% of the records to `r pct(num)`% of the
individuals, because `r pct(100 * mal_multi, 0)`% of the malacostracan records
with a count hold more than one individual. The unidentified
material falls out almost entirely: it rarely has a count, and records without
a count contribute nothing to %N (`dv_tree()` warns, here about
`r sum(is.na(cod$prey_count))` cod records). The default currency is records
for that reason.

## Checking a table against a specification

`dv_validate()` stops if a declared column is missing, if there is no prey key
column, or if a weight is negative. It warns about records with no prey key,
weights that are not numbers and stomach IDs shared between predators, and it
ends with a one-line description of the sample. It reports problems and never
changes your data. It returns the data invisibly, so you can use it in a
pipeline.

```{r validate}
invisible(dv_validate(dat, spec))
```

## Mapping your own survey

To use DietView on another table, write a different `dv_spec()`. If your
columns were `sp`, `stom`, `aphia`, `wt_g` and `yr`, you would write:

```{r own, eval = FALSE}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator = "sp", stomach = "stom", prey_id = "aphia",
  weight = "wt_g", covariates = "yr"
)
```

The later steps (`dv_prepare()`, `dv_build_tree()`, `dv_sunburst()`,
`dv_build_html()`) read the column names from the specification, never from
your code. The article "Adapting DietView to your own survey" goes through
the other choices you make with a new table.
